abstract: Diseases that disrupt dopamine impair cognition; however, it is unknown how dopamine affects neuronal networks that instantiate cognitive processing. We studied this problem in the dorsomedial striatum during interval timing, an elementary cognitive task requiring working memory and attention to estimate an interval of several seconds. Interval timing requires medium spiny neurons (MSNs) that ramp up or down over temporal intervals. While these neurons receive prominent dopaminergic input from the substantia nigra, it is unknown how dopamine modulates MSN activity during interval timing. Here, we report four new findings. First, ramping activity of MSN ensembles predicts interval timing behavior. Second, dopamine dynamics predict timing behavior and preferentially predict the slope of MSN ensembles that ramp down; these relationships are not observed during tasks without temporal control such as Pavlovian conditioning. Third, inactivating substantia nigra dopamine disrupts timing as well as MSNs that ramp down, but not those that ramp up. Fourth, a drift-diffusion model perturbing down-ramping accurately predicted interval timing behavior in mice with dopamine inhibition and in humans with Parkinson's disease. Together, these results reveal how dopamine shapes striatal ramping dynamics and suggest that disrupting dopamine can alter specific trajectories of cognitive computations. These data are relevant for understanding the cognitive striatum and for generating new markers and therapeutic strategies for human striatal and dopaminergic diseases.
